title: Adolescence
summary: Adolescence is the period of development between childhood and adulthood (WHO: 10–19 years; the eventful years are 11–18). Puberty, at about 11–12 years and lasting about 2 years, marks the beginning, with a growth spurt and appearance of sex characteristics; the first sign in girls is menstruation (menarche) and in boys nocturnal emission. Girls: gain about 8 cm height at 11–13½ years, more fatty tissue and rounded contours, slender shoulders and broad rounded hips, hair in armpits and pubic area, shrill adult-like voice, breast bud. Boys: gain about 20 cm at 13–15 years, more muscle, broader shoulders and slender hips, darker curly body hair and facial hair, the voice breaks (larynx enlarges, Adam's apple), growth of the penis and first nocturnal emission about a year later. Girls reach adult height, weight and ability to bear children about two years earlier than boys.

Early-maturing girls feel conscious and odd and are expected to behave responsibly; late-maturing girls are relaxed but get little attention from boys. Early-maturing boys are confident, chosen as leaders but face high adult expectations; late-maturing boys feel inferior. These feelings are temporary; parents should explain the changes and give sex education.

Adolescents have mood swings in early years because of hormones, like to be with the peer group (its own culture, values, language, dress and music) and conform to group norms; one unable to make friends may become depressed. Language: fluent and complex; characteristic features are slang (e.g. 'bindaas') and short forms or abbreviations (CP for Connaught Place). Cognitive: thinking becomes abstract; the adolescent can imagine situations, think contrary to fact ('if we could all fly'), understand similes and abstract jokes, conclude A is bigger than C without seeing the objects and weigh all alternatives, so thinking is mature and systematic.

By the end of adolescence the person is sexually mature and should be prepared for marriage and family life; attitudes to sex determine adult sexual behaviour (education for reproductive health). Peers and printed material often give wrong information and misconceptions, so parents should build a wholesome relationship so that the adolescent can ask questions and get right answers.
## Role of parents, peers and school

Parents: adolescents want independence yet depend on parents. Parents who give freedom and take interest produce independent, responsible adolescents; very strict, authoritarian parents hamper independence; indifferent parents produce indifferent adolescents; parents who involve and value opinions produce confident children. Peers: a shift from parents to the peer group at 14–16 years, especially in nuclear families; peers share the same conflicts, give a chance to learn to interact with the opposite sex and set the 'peer culture' (dress, speech). Peer culture is a way of feeling different from parents; parents should watch for anti-social activities (gangs, violence); peers can reinforce parental values or exert harmful pressure (drugs, shoplifting) or positive influence (studying hard). School and teachers: a school that is not harsh and respects students, with trained, warm and enthusiastic teachers, brings out the best; poor teachers cause loss of interest and drop-outs; the teacher can bridge the generation gap.

Developmental tasks: accepting one's physique, more mature relationships with age-mates of both sexes, achieving a masculine or feminine social role, emotional independence from parents, achieving a set of values, preparing for a career and preparing for marriage and family life. Typical characteristics: preoccupation with looks (feeling 'on stage'), peer group culture, 'crushes' on much older persons of the opposite sex, idealism, rebellion, generation gap, mood swings, being easily influenced and identity formation ('Who am I?'). Problems: eating disorders (undereating, overeating, vomiting), suicidal tendencies (loneliness), peer pressure (alcohol, smoking, drugs), personal problems about looks, social problems, biological problems (girls hesitate to ask; need counselling) and teenage pregnancy. Legal age of marriage: 18 for girls and 21 for boys. Early pregnancy damages the reproductive tract, babies are underweight and likely to die, the large family size and curtailed education reduce quality of life.

objective: State True or False. (i) At 16 years Rahul will get hair on his face. (ii) Priya will gain 2 cm height at the age of 12. (iii) Nocturnal emission is normal for boys. (iv) Most girls and boys suffer from acne during adolescence.
(i) True. (ii) False: girls gain about 8 cm in the year. (iii) True. (iv) True.

Give reasons for the following behaviour of adolescents: (i) worry about their looks (ii) peculiar talking and dressing (iii) intense love towards a much older person of the opposite sex (iv) feel parents do not understand them.
(i) Rapid body changes make them feel 'on stage'. (ii) They follow the peer group culture. (iii) It is a 'crush', a typical stage. (iv) Rebellion and the generation gap.

vsa: Explain why adolescents need proper sex education and what role parents can play.
Adolescents become sexually mature and peers and printed matter give wrong information. Parents should build an open relationship and give correct answers to their questions.

or: Describe the typical characteristics of adolescent thinking that distinguish it from childhood thinking.
Adolescents think abstractly and can imagine and think contrary to fact ideas. They consider all alternatives and understand similes and abstract jokes, unlike children who need to see things.

vsa: Explain the effects of early maturation in adolescent boys and girls.
Early maturing boys are confident and chosen as leaders but adults expect more from them. Early maturing girls feel conscious and odd and are expected to behave like adults.
Why is peer group important to adolescents? Give two reasons.
Everybody has the same conflicts and peers seem more understanding than parents. It lets them learn to interact with the opposite sex and follow peer culture.
List two harmful effects of peer pressure.
Adolescents may be pressurised to try drugs, alcohol or smoking. They may shoplift or act against their own judgement and later regret it.
Eating disorders such as undereating or overeating and suicidal tendencies from loneliness. Peer pressure and teenage pregnancy are also problems.
sa: Explain the effect of early and late maturation on adolescents (three points).

(i) Early maturing girls feel conscious and odd, while late maturing girls are relaxed but ignored by boys. (ii) Early maturing boys are confident leaders. (iii) Late maturing boys feel inferior; these feelings are temporary and parents should explain the changes.
Discuss the various ways in which parents discipline adolescents (three points).

(i) Giving freedom with interest develops independence and responsibility. (ii) Strict, authoritative control hampers independence. (iii) Indifference gives indifferent children, so respect and love are best.
Explain the role of the school in adolescence (three points).

(i) A school that is not harsh and respects students' views makes them enjoy studies. (ii) Warm trained teachers recognise talents and motivate; poor teachers lead to drop-outs. (iii) Teachers can bridge the generation gap.
Enumerate three developmental tasks of adolescence.
(i) Accepting one's physique and using it effectively. (ii) Achieving emotional independence from parents. (iii) Achieving a set of values and preparing for a career and family life.
la: Explain the physical, social and cognitive changes of adolescence, and the problems adolescents face.

(i) Boys grow muscles, broad shoulders, facial hair and their voice breaks; girls get rounded contours, broad hips and menarche. (ii) Girls mature about two years earlier than boys. (iii) Socially they prefer the peer group and its culture. (iv) Thinking becomes abstract and systematic. (v) Typical features are preoccupation with looks, crushes, idealism, rebellion and mood swings. (vi) Problems include eating disorders, suicidal tendencies, peer pressure, biological problems and teenage pregnancy.
